Soft MPCritic: Amortized Model Predictive Value Iteration

Thomas Banker    Nathan P. Lawrence    Ali Mesbah ††thanks: The authors are with the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA. mesbah@berkeley.edu††thanks: This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences under award DE‐SC0024472.
Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) and model predictive control (MPC) offer complementary strengths, yet combining them at scale remains computationally challenging. We propose soft MPCritic, an RL-MPC framework that learns in (soft) value space while using sample-based planning for both online control and value target generation. soft MPCritic instantiates MPC through model predictive path integral control (MPPI) and trains a terminal 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function with fitted value iteration, aligning the learned value function with the planner and implicitly extending the effective planning horizon. We introduce an amortized warm-start strategy that recycles planned open-loop action sequences from online observations when computing batched MPPI-based value targets. This makes soft MPCritic computationally practical, while preserving solution quality. soft MPCritic plans in a scenario-based fashion with an ensemble of dynamic models trained for next-step prediction accuracy. Together, these ingredients enable soft MPCritic to learn effectively through robust, short-horizon planning on classic and complex control tasks. These results establish soft MPCritic as a practical and scalable blueprint for synthesizing MPC policies in settings where policy extraction and direct, long-horizon planning may fail.

I Introduction

Reinforcement learning and model predictive control are contrasting strategies for designing decision-making agents. Model predictive control accounts for system dynamics and constraints to construct a notion of value to be optimized online in a receding-horizon fashion [1]. Meanwhile, a core design philosophy driving (actor-critic) reinforcement learning methods is value-based backup followed by policy extraction [2, 3]. There are pros and cons to both approaches, as discussed below. Nevertheless, reinforcement learning and model predictive control offer complementary benefits, motivating hybrid frameworks that incorporate planning into a flexible learning pipeline [4, 5].

There is a plethora of ways in which dynamic models can be integrated into reinforcement learning [6]. One useful way to divide them is based on alignment: does the reinforcement learning agent learn from the model or does the model learn from the agent? The so-called “dyna” framework is a popular instance of the former. Here, simulated experience is used to train a policy using otherwise model-free algorithms. This strategy can be very sample efficient [7], but has also been shown to be brittle due to its over reliance on simulated experience [8, 9]. Other lines of work use a model to construct a value target or loss for policy learning [10, 11, 12]. These approaches provide a rich loss landscape for policy learning; however, it may be difficult to optimize. Model predictive control has also been shown to be a useful structure within reinforcement learning. If the model is sufficiently accurate, then reinforcement learning can provide model predictive control with a terminal value function [4], a baseline policy [13, 14], or model predictive control can provide model-based value targets for training a critic network [15]. The other end of the spectrum aims to learn a dynamic model that aligns with the reward or value function [16, 17]. This can also take the form of differentiable model predictive control wherein the planner is differentiated and updated to maximize some objective [18, 19]. Model predictive control is viewed as a function approximator whose parameters (including the dynamic model) can be shaped to suit the control objective. In principle, there is significant flexibility in this approach, but it can be hindered by computational and feasibility issues [5].

We propose a hybrid model predictive control-reinforcement learning framework inspired by soft value iteration [20, 21]. A dynamic model is used only for short-term predictions within a value-augmented model predictive control. This model predictive control serves two functions: control and value function training. To train the terminal value function, the model predictive control itself provides temporal difference-style targets. This procedure aligns the terminal value function with the model predictive control, implicitly extending its horizon for online decision-making. We call this framework soft MPCritic, representing a parallel work to MPCritic [22]. MPCritic follows an actor-critic design, wherein a “fictitious” controller serves as an approximate model predictive control solution to streamline the integration of model predictive control within reinforcement learning without explicitly solving model predictive control or computing its sensitivities for reinforcement learning updates. In contrast, soft MPCritic lives entirely in value space. Specifically, we formalize soft MPCritic in the context of soft value iteration wherein a softmax-like operation is used in place of hard maximization as in classical dynamic programming [23]. This formulation naturally connects model predictive control, specifically model predictive path integral control [24, 25, 26], to soft value iteration and enables efficient integration of model predictive control within a reinforcement learning pipeline. soft MPCritic is designed to be algorithmically simple, emphasizing the utility of short-horizon planning and value iteration, while mapping out possible extensions for future work. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    An reinforcement learning-model predictive control algorithm that lives entirely in value space, utilizing a formal connection between path integral control and soft value iteration.

  2. 2.

    An amortized value iteration approach to efficient model predictive control integration within reinforcement learning. Specifically, we disperse the computational burden of model predictive control via a warm-starting strategy both for online and offline target value generation.

  3. 3.

    Case studies demonstrating the soft MPCritic on challenging control problems and validating the use of a planner both for online control and target generation.

II Problem setting

II-A Markov decision processes

We consider a Markov decision process comprising an environment and agent. The environment has states s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} that evolve randomly as actions a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} are proposed by the agent. We assume these state transitions are Markovian and characterized by a probability density pp; mathematically, s′∼p(s′|s,a)s^{\prime}\sim p\left(s^{\prime}\middle|s,a\right), where s′∈𝒮s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S} denotes a next state.

States and actions are scored with a cost function ℓ:𝒮×𝒜→ℝ\ell:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}. The agent should design actions that account for the cumulative cost of its actions. As a reference, we first examine the so-called free energy of the system. The free energy considers an open-loop prior β~\tilde{\beta} over actions and the cost of the resulting trajectories. We denote the induced distribution over trajectories by τ∼pβ~\tau\sim p^{\tilde{\beta}}, where τ={s0,a0,…,sH−1,aH−1}\tau=\{s_{0},a_{0},\ldots,s_{H-1},a_{H-1}\}. Note τ\tau depends only on the initial state distribution and sequences of actions, denoted by α={a0,…,aH−1}\alpha=\{a_{0},\ldots,a_{H-1}\}, meaning we can write τ=τ⁡(α,s0)\tau=\tau(\alpha,s_{0}). Taking JJ to be a real-valued function measuring cumulative cost, the free energy is defined as

ℱ=−λ​log⁡(𝔼τ∼pβ~​[exp⁡(−1λ​J​(τ))]),\mathcal{F}=-\lambda\log\left(\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p^{\tilde{\beta}}}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}J(\tau)\right)\right]\right),\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:free_{e}nergy} (2)

where λ>0\lambda>0 is a temperature parameter and s0∼p⁡(s0)s_{0}\sim p(s_{0}). Intuitively, free energy is a soft minimum over random trajectories; λ\lambda influences the sharpness of the soft minimum operator and β~\tilde{\beta} determines the scope and texture of the action space.

For any distribution over actions β\beta, it can be shown (by Jensen’s inequality) that

ℱ≤−λ​𝔼τ∼pβ​[log⁡(∏t=0H−1β~​(at)β⁡(at)​exp⁡(−1λ​J​(τ)))].\mathcal{F}\leq-\lambda\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p^{\beta}}\left[\log\left(\prod_{t=0}^{H-1}\frac{\tilde{\beta}(a_{t})}{\beta(a_{t})}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}J(\tau)\right)\right)\right]. (3)

Given this lower bound, and with a slight abuse of notation, it can be verified that the optimal distribution has density

β⋆​(α)=1η​exp⁡(−1λ​J​(τ))​∏t=0H−1β~​(at),\beta^{\star}(\alpha)=\frac{1}{\eta}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}J(\tau)\right)\prod_{t=0}^{H-1}\tilde{\beta}(a_{t}),\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:opt_{p}df} (4)

where η\eta is a normalizing constant. While 4 gives an elegant solution to the problem, sampling directly from β⋆\beta^{\star} is infeasible. The goal of the agent is to design a near-optimal control distribution over actions that approximately matches the free energy of the system. Next, we outline two methodological frameworks for this problem.

II-B Path integral control approach

Model predictive path integral control approximately samples from β⋆\beta^{\star} through importance sampling and Monte Carlo estimation [24, 25, 27]. To begin, model predictive path integral control aims to find optimal control inputs that minimize the KL divergence between the optimal distribution β⋆\beta^{\star} and the design distribution β\beta. The principal result is that the optimal control inputs can be expressed as an expectation of weighted actions over β\beta

ut⋆=1η​𝔼α∼β⁡(α)​[w⁡(α)​at].u_{t}^{\star}=\frac{1}{\eta}\mathbb{E}_{\alpha\sim\beta(\alpha)}\left[w(\alpha)a_{t}\right]. (5)

Assuming, as a standard example, β~=𝒩⁡(0,Σ)\tilde{\beta}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) and β=𝒩⁡(u,Σ)\beta=\mathcal{N}(u,\Sigma), where uu is a commanded control input, actions are sampled through the change of variables a=u+ϵa=u+\epsilon. Sampling NN noise sequences ε(n)={ϵ0(n),…,ϵH−1(n)}\varepsilon^{(n)}=\{\epsilon_{0}^{(n)},\ldots,\epsilon_{H-1}^{(n)}\}, the (unnormalized) weights are given by

w⁡(ε(n))=exp⁡(−1λ​(J⁡(τ⁡(υ+ε(n),s0))CLOSECLOSE+λ2∑t=0H−1ut⊤Σ−1(ut+2ϵt(n)))),w(\varepsilon^{(n)})=\exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\Big(J\big(\tau(\upsilon+\varepsilon^{(n)},s_{0})\big)\\ +\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}u_{t}^{{}^{\top}}\Sigma^{-1}\big(u_{t}+2\epsilon_{t}^{(n)}\big)\Big)\bigg), (6)

where s0∼p⁡(s0)s_{0}\sim p(s_{0}) and υ={u0,…,uH−1}\upsilon=\{u_{0},\ldots,u_{H-1}\} and the (approximate) normalization constant in 4 is given by

η=1N​∑n=1Nw⁡(ε(n)).\eta=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(\varepsilon^{(n)}). (7)

This weighted structure highlights low-cost trajectories and ignores “bad” ones. Control inputs are then updated iteratively

ut(i+1)=ut(i)+1η​N​∑n=1Nw⁡(ε(n))​ϵt(n).u^{(i+1)}_{t}=u^{(i)}_{t}+\frac{1}{\eta N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(\varepsilon^{(n)})\epsilon_{t}^{(n)}.\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:u_{i}ter} (8)

Model predictive path integral control is implemented in a receding-horizon fashion, meaning the online policy applies u0(⋅)u^{(\cdot)}_{0}, the first action computed in 8, and then the model predictive path integral control steps are repeated at the next state.

II-C Soft value function approach

We introduce a state-dependent free energy mirroring 2. The soft value function at state ss is defined as

𝒱⁡(s)=−λlog(𝔼τ∼pβ~[exp(−1λ∑t=0∞γtℓ(st,at))|s0=s]),\mathcal{V}(s)=\\ -\lambda\log\left(\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p^{\tilde{\beta}}}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\ell(s_{t},a_{t})\right)\middle|s_{0}=s\right]\right),\ignorespaces\ignorespaces (9)

where 0<γ<10<\gamma<1 is a fixed discount factor [20, 21]. 𝒱\mathcal{V} is near identical to ℱ\mathcal{F} except it evaluates the free energy at a desired state; in that way, ℱ=𝔼s0∼p⁡(s0)​[𝒱⁡(s0)]\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim p(s_{0})}\left[\mathcal{V}(s_{0})\right]. Value functions enable iterative solution methods that decompose the infinite-horizon objective into recursive subproblems [28, 23]. It is helpful to introduce the soft action-value function or 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function, which follows the same definition as 𝒱\mathcal{V} except it is initialized at state-action pairs. A concise way of expressing 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is in terms of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, i.e.,

𝒬(s,a)=ℓ(s,a)+γ𝔼s′∼p(s′|s,a)[𝒱(s′)].\mathcal{Q}(s,a)=\ell(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim p\left(s^{\prime}\middle|s,a\right)}\left[\mathcal{V}(s^{\prime})\right].\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:soft_{b}ellman} (10)

𝒬\mathcal{Q} enables the agent to design a single action that accounts for long-term cost, captured by the expected free energy across next possible states. Note 10 can be written with 𝒬\mathcal{Q} on both sides of the equation, leading to a soft Bellman optimality equation. Therefore, one may take 𝒬\mathcal{Q} to be an objective function to be (softly) optimized, for example, using distribution matching technique of the previous section (take J=𝒬J=\mathcal{Q}). Proceeding along this path, we have α=a\alpha=a and arrive at at the optimal distribution

π⋆​(a|s)\displaystyle\pi^{\star}\left(a\middle|s\right) =1η​exp⁡(−1λ​𝒬​(s,a))​β~​(a)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\eta}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\mathcal{Q}(s,a)\right)\tilde{\beta}(a) (11)
∝exp⁡(−1λ​(𝒬⁡(s,a)−𝒱⁡(s))−‖a‖Σ−12),\displaystyle\propto\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(\mathcal{Q}(s,a)-\mathcal{V}(s)\right)-\mathchoice{\left\|{{{{a}}}}\right\|}{\|{{{{a}}}}\|}{\|{{{{a}}}}\|}{\|{{{{a}}}}\|}_{\Sigma^{-1}}^{2}\right), (12)

as 𝒱⁡(s)=−λ​log⁡(η)\mathcal{V}(s)=-\lambda\log(\eta). Therefore, π⋆\pi^{\star} optimally balances the advantage of each action over the state value 𝒱\mathcal{V} and control effort.

III soft MPCritic framework

III-A Ethos of MPCritic

The goal of MPCritic [22] is to enable efficient integration of model predictive control and reinforcement learning through principled approximations. MPCritic follows an actor-critic strategy. The actor, or a subset of its parameters, are trained to approximately represent the solution to a model predictive control problem. This uses the differentiable predictive control method [10] in an iterative, online training context. This (approximate) model predictive control-enabled actor works in tandem with a critic network to approximate model predictive control value targets. A full model predictive control is then used online, where exactness and constraint satisfaction are most important and expensive.

soft MPCritic is another realization of this goal, rather than an extension of MPCritic. While MPCritic emphasizes deterministic model predictive control, classical dynamic programming principles, and applications where constraints are critical, soft MPCritic emphasizes scalability, motivating sample-based model predictive control and soft value functions. We develop an algorithm that leverages sample-based model predictive control for both online control and value target generation, as illustrated in Fig. 1. This strategy “aligns” the model predictive control and its terminal value function, which makes it possible to leverage a dynamic model trained only on one-step transitions. We further show how this setup is computationally efficient by spreading out the model predictive control target computation over the course of training.

III-B Fitted 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-iteration via MPPI

The (idealized) architecture used in soft MPCritic is

𝒱MPPI​(s)≈−λ​log⁡(𝔼τψ∼pβ~​[exp⁡(−1λ​Jϕ​(τψ))|s0=s]),\mathcal{V}^{\text{MPPI}}(s)\approx-\lambda\log\left(\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{\psi}\sim p^{\tilde{\beta}}}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\lambda}J_{\phi}(\tau_{\psi})\right)\middle|s_{0}=s\right]\right),\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:mppi_{v}alue} (13)

where Jϕ​(τψ)=∑t=0H−1γt​ℓ​(st,at)+γH​𝒬ϕ​(sH,aH)J_{\phi}(\tau_{\psi})=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\ell(s_{t},a_{t})+\gamma^{H}\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}(s_{H},a_{H}) and τψ\tau_{\psi} refers to trajectories under a learnable model fψf_{\psi}. fψf_{\psi} is trained to minimize the mean squared error between its prediction and the observed next state; however, other objectives or multi-step targets may be used. We find it beneficial to mitigate uncertainty in ψ\psi by training an ensemble of dynamic models. Model predictive path integral control therefore considers a branching dynamic model of the form

ψ\displaystyle\psi ∼p⁡(ψ)\displaystyle\sim p(\psi) (14)
s′\displaystyle s^{\prime} =fψ​(s,a),\displaystyle=f_{\psi}(s,a), (15)

where models ψ\psi are sampled uniformly. Concurrently, 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} is trained to approximately solve the (soft) Bellman equation, namely, 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} should be such that 𝒱MPPI≈𝒱\mathcal{V}^{\text{MPPI}}\approx\mathcal{V} in the infinite-horizon definition in . Fitted 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-iteration is an iterative technique for training 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}; it was introduced by [29] and made tractable in high-dimensional continuous spaces by [2]. Here, we use it as an umbrella term, as it is a prevalent idea and this work is compatible with the stabilization techniques introduced since the nominal algorithm of [29].

We define the objective

ℒ𝒬=MSE​(𝒬ϕ,ℓ+γ​𝒱MPPI),\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\text{MSE}\left(\mathcal{Q}_{\phi},\ell+\gamma\mathcal{V}^{\text{MPPI}}\right),\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:qfun_{o}bj} (16)

where the mean squared error is computed over a batch from the replay buffer 𝒟\mathcal{D} containing tuples of the form (s,a,ℓ,s′,υ)(s,a,\ell,s^{\prime},\upsilon). ℓ\ell is the observed cost at s,as,a and 𝒱MPPI\mathcal{V}^{\text{MPPI}} is the model predictive path integral control value in 13 evaluated at s′s^{\prime}. Equation 16 is only a nominal objective, as variations involving double or target 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-networks are possible [2, 3]. If H=0H=0 in 𝒱MPPI\mathcal{V}^{\text{MPPI}}, then 16 will be a soft version of classical fitted 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-iteration powered by model predictive path integral control, marking a conceptual similarity to soft actor-critic [3]. Taking H>0H>0 embeds short-horizon model information into the targets. This same model predictive path integral control is used for online control, making 𝒬\mathcal{Q} aligned with the model-based model predictive path integral control value estimate and implicitly extending its prediction horizon. The weights ϕ\phi are updated iteratively using some form of gradient descent as new data is added to the replay buffer. υ\upsilon is included in the replay tuples to make the model predictive path integral control target computationally efficient.

III-C Amortized soft MPCritic algorithm

The number of trajectory samples is a potential bottleneck for any algorithm involving model predictive path integral control, such as soft MPCritic. Precise control quickly becomes infeasible as H→∞H\rightarrow\infty, meaning the number of trajectories is coupled with the prediction horizon. soft MPCritic addresses this by fixing the prediction horizon and caching long-horizon planning with terminal 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function, i.e., 13. This enables precise control aimed at global optimality with a tractable number of planning trajectories. Algorithm 1 is a generic instantiation of this, which can be expanded to incorporate covariance and/or temperature annealing [27], baseline policies [14, 13], non-Gaussian distributions, and other recent advancements in model predictive path integral control [26].

While a terminal 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function can alleviate sampling challenges during online control, it shifts the burden of computation to 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-iteration. Furthermore, for Algorithm 1 to be successful online, 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} should be aligned with the model predictive path integral control controller, motivating the use of model predictive path integral control for both online control and in reinforcement learning updates. Considering a fixed number of trajectory samples, the cost of reinforcement learning scales with the number of value iteration steps though. soft MPCritic addresses this issue by amortizing target computations at each value iteration step. Recall 8 is an iterative update rule. Thus, the model predictive path integral control optimization for reinforcement learning updates need not start from scratch; open-loop controls υ\upsilon calculated online can be recycled for target computation. This inspires the proposed warm-starting strategy for target computations, exemplified in Algorithm 2.

The benefits of warm-starting targets as in Algorithm 2 include: 1) fewer trajectory samples needed for reinforcement learning updates; and 2) targets are iteratively refined as learning proceeds. Regarding the former, online control demands a sizable number of trajectories to acquire near optimal solutions. Hence, when applied to target initialization, only minor refinement is typically necessary. These refinements occur each time a tuple (s,a,ℓ,s′,υ)(s,a,\ell,s^{\prime},\upsilon) is sampled from the replay buffer, meaning υ\upsilon adapts with the model and terminal value function throughout training.

Empirically, we observe that warm-starting model predictive path integral control targets can be highly effective; with only ≈10%\approx 10\% of samples used online, significantly reducing the computational cost of the reinforcement learning algorithm. This can be explained through the weighted structure behind 8. Consider two samples ε(j)\varepsilon^{(j)} and ε(i)\varepsilon^{(i)}, which are relatively small compared to open-loop controls υ\upsilon, giving the ratio of weights

w⁡(ε(j))w⁡(ε(i))≈exp⁡(−1λ​(J⁡(τ⁡(υ+ε(j),s0))−J⁡(τ⁡(υ+ε(i),s0)))).\frac{w(\varepsilon^{(j)})}{w(\varepsilon^{(i)})}\approx\\ \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{\lambda}\Big(J\big(\tau(\upsilon+\varepsilon^{(j)},s_{0})\big)-J\big(\tau(\upsilon+\varepsilon^{(i)},s_{0})\big)\Big)\bigg). (17)

The weight ratio ensures that even a linear increase in cost JJ results in an exponential decrease in influence when updating υ\upsilon. The risk of all samples increasing the cost—thereby degrading υ\upsilon—can be mitigated without increasing sample size by annealing the covariance. Furthermore, as part of the latter benefit, any suboptimal updates are naturally corrected in subsequent iterations, as previous target solutions are recycled to warm-start the optimization. Reusing target solutions in subsequent iterations also helps prevent υ\upsilon from becoming stale as 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} is continually updated. Thus, amortization via warm-started targets yields substantial computational savings without significantly compromising the overall reinforcement learning algorithm’s performance.

III-D Broader scope of soft MPCritic

soft MPCritic lives in soft value space; however, it could also be adapted to a traditional dynamic programming setting. This can be accomplished by targeting the usual Bellman optimality equation. Further, the resulting value function-augmented model predictive control would directly minimize cost under the system model. Nonetheless, model predictive path integral control is useful in the soft MPCritic framework for several reasons. The model is learned online in tandem with the value function, meaning exact minimization may be detrimental to overall stability and performance over the course of training. Additionally, model predictive path integral control is agnostic to model and value networks, making it very scalable, a key bottleneck in the reinforcement learning-model predictive control interface [5]. Therefore, while model predictive path integral control is suboptimal relative to a deterministic optimal control problem [27], its benefits are worthwhile.

IV Case studies

soft MPCritic is tested on two case studies. The first demonstrates the benefits of amortizing the 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-iteration process with soft MPCritic on a classical control environment, measuring computational efficiency and reward as a proxy for solution quality. The second ablates soft MPCritic on a challenging robotics environment, establishing the importance of a terminal value function, modeling uncertainty in the dynamics, and planning for control and target computation. The finalized version is benchmarked relative to standard reinforcement learning algorithms.11 1 Code is available at: https://github.com/NPLawrence/soft-mpcritic

IV-A Amortization in Learning

Here, soft MPCritic is evaluated in an online learning setting with unknown dynamics, but known goal of balancing a double inverted pendulum. All learnable components of soft MPCritic, 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} and fψf_{\psi}, are parameterized as neural networks. We analyze the effects of warm-starting and using an ensemble of dynamics models in terms of computation and performance.

The grid of plots in Fig. 2 displays the performance of four learning configurations for soft MPCritic, a full factorial design. As seen in the left-hand plots, soft MPCritic with warm-starting quickly maximizes the reward in almost every seed. This is in stark contrast with cold starting model predictive path integral control for computing 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function targets in the right-hand plots. Cold starting these computations generally increases variance in the learning process but, if given enough iterations, can achieve similarly rewarding solutions. However, this comes with additional compute, whereas warm-starting can recycle the online solution and continually refine it. In this way, the open-loop controls υ\upsilon stored in the replay buffer are iteratively updated to best approximate the optimal sequence for the current 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} and fψf_{\psi}. Hence, in this example, only a single iteration is necessary to (approximately) maximize performance, roughly matching that of soft actor-critic.

While not always a major difference for this simpler system, using a single dynamic model can result in suboptimal solutions when warm or cold starting. This can be attributed to compounding prediction errors over the planning horizon, which manifests in both value function learning and online control to ultimately hinder performance. Rather, planning over an ensemble provides a degree of robustness to parametric uncertainties, meaning model predictive path integral control favors low-cost trajectories with high agreement among the ensemble. As seen in Fig. 2, this robustness can aid in tightening the range of rewards when warm-starting. This point is revisited in the next case study where the effects become more pronounced in high-dimensional environments, which can be challenging to accurately model.

Warm-starting can achieve comparable performance to cold starting, but its greatest utility is possibly in amortizing the cost of the overall reinforcement learning algorithm. This effect is measured and tabulated in Table I, comparing the environment steps per second relative to cold starting. As the number of model predictive path integral control rollouts NN used for target computation increase, all approaches experience a degree of slow down. However, recalling Fig. 2, cold starting requires ≥5\geq 5 iterations to achieve comparable performance to 11 iteration when warm-starting. Requiring additional iterations brings the unfavorable scaling of cold starting to the forefront. Achieving similar performance with cold starting amounts to a ≥50%\geq 50\% slow down in wall time, depending on the desired solution quality. Hence, we only consider warm-starting target computation for all further experiments for its computational efficiency with minimal sacrifice to performance.

IV-B High-dimensional Control

To distinguish the critical design choices behind soft MPCritic, we ablate the approach on a more challenging robotics problem. Here, we consider the Hopper-v5 environment with unknown dynamics but known goal of maximizing velocity while remaining upright. Preserving all hyperparameters from the previous case study, we ablate the model predictive path integral control formulation and its usage throughout Algorithm 2. In terms of formulation, we gauge the impact of the terminal 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function and revisit the benefits of modeling parametric uncertainties with an ensemble. Regarding model predictive path integral control’s usage, we separately compare substituting a parametric representation, i.e., a neural network as is standard in reinforcement learning, for online decision-making or 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function target computation.

Starting with the left panel of Fig. 3, we can begin to distill the essential model predictive path integral control ingredients. If the terminal 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function is removed such that only the dynamics ensemble remains (denoted as “no 𝒬\mathcal{Q} / ff Ensemble” in Fig. 3), performance collapses. This is to be expected as the 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function implicitly extends the model predictive path integral control planning horizon, and without it, planning is confined to a finite horizon (H=8H=8 in this case). Without knowing the true dynamics, extending HH further to mitigate this effect is not guaranteed to address this issue. That is not to say the value learning underpinning soft MPCritic is not also vulnerable to model mismatch. This is most evident when we remove the dynamics model ensemble from the model predictive path integral control formulation (denoted as “𝒬\mathcal{Q} / no ff Ensemble” in Fig. 3). Learning and optimizing the terminal 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function under the predictions of an erroneous model can hinder performance as indicated by the cumulative reward. Incorporating an ensemble targets this very weakness, as the 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function is learned to reflect uncertainty in the dynamics, and trajectories are planned subject to this uncertainty.

Moving to the right panel of Fig. 3, we examine where in Algorithm 2 it is crucial to utilize model predictive path integral control. We compare to substituting model predictive path integral control with a neural network policy μ\mu with parameters θ\theta learned such that μθ​(s)≈arg​mina⁡𝒬ϕ​(s,a)\mu_{\theta}(s)\approx\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{a}\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}(s,a).22 2 Instead of this DDPG-style strategy, we also tested the use of model predictive path integral control for optimizing 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} alone, that is, without any planning; the results were similar and the conclusions in this ablations still held true. To begin with, we ask if it is sufficient to only use model predictive path integral control for online control (denoted as “Control” in Fig. 3), effectively replacing line 10 of Algorithm 2 with 𝒱⁡(s)←𝒬⁡(s,μθ​(s))\mathcal{V}(s)\leftarrow\mathcal{Q}(s,\mu_{\theta}(s)). In the early stages of learning, performance is similar to the full model predictive path integral control algorithm; both algorithms benefit from online re-planning despite their initially poor 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-function approximators. However, as learning progresses, misalignment between the neural network policy objective and the true form of the optimal policy π⋆​(a|s)\pi^{\star}\left(a\middle|s\right) hinders value learning, and thus, performance. If we only use model predictive path integral control for target computation in Algorithm 2 (denoted as “Targets” in Fig. 3), the misalignment of μθ\mu_{\theta} also manifests. Compounding this fact, μθ\mu_{\theta} does not benefit from re-planning during online control, and the performance of μθ\mu_{\theta} is largely dependent on its extraction algorithm from 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}. Using model predictive path integral control for both tasks ensures alignment between online control and learning, and benefits from online re-planning without requiring additional policy function approximators.

Having settled on these algorithmic primitives, we compare the full soft MPCritic algorithm with standard reinforcement learning baselines, soft actor-critic and deep deterministic policy gradient. soft actor-critic is included due to its shared roots in soft value-iteration. We include DDPG because of its algorithmic simplicity; omitting techniques such as double 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-networks and temperature auto-tuning utilized by soft actor-critic but not by Algorithm 2. For conceptual alignment, we deploy Algorithm 1 with a uniform prior such that soft MPCritic, like soft actor-critic, is optimizing a Gaussian control distribution for maximum entropy control. Results can be seen in Fig. 4. Notably, soft MPCritic exceeds the asymptotic performance of both baselines (measured at 10610^{6} time steps) within the first 2×1052\times 10^{5} time steps. With all algorithms sharing the same 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-iteration frequency and aligned objectives, the primary distinction of the proposed approach apart is the model predictive path integral control planning module. As compared to soft actor-critic, HH-step predictions aid in generating quality soft value function targets, accelerating value learning. Furthermore, online re-planning enables the agent to adapt its behavior based on feedback while avoiding parametric policy extraction as a learning bottleneck. With the planner aligned for both value estimation and control, soft MPCritic offers a streamlined yet high-performance approach to control.

V Conclusions

soft MPCritic is an algorithmic framework for learning model predictive control in value space via reinforcement learning. In this work, soft MPCritic does not leverage specialized model learning objectives and many of the stabilization techniques common in deep reinforcement learning, yet still achieves strong performance. Specifically, soft MPCritic learns a high-quality value function that enables effective short-horizon planning in settings where the same model fails under direct planning—highlighting the benefit of value-space learning over open-loop rollouts. Our results establish soft MPCritic as a principled foundation for future work, including incorporation of advanced model learning objectives, stability guarantees, and broader model predictive control-enabled reinforcement learning algorithm design.
